Chapter 3: Melancholy as a Shared Experience
There’s a certain kind of sadness you’ll find only in Istanbul. It’s almost like a gentle fog that never really lifts—a feeling locals call hüzün. But here’s what makes it unique: it isn’t just something people feel on their own. This melancholy is shared, connecting folks from all walks of life, across generations and neighborhoods. It’s part of the city’s heartbeat, shaping how people see themselves and the world around them.
Picture the city in those early morning hours, when everything is hushed and the streets seem to be holding their breath. That’s when this feeling is at its strongest. You notice it in the peeling paint on old buildings, in the slow, thoughtful movements of shopkeepers as they unlock their doors, even in the distant sound of a ferry’s horn cutting through the mist. For many, hüzün brings a strange kind of comfort. It’s a quiet reminder that they’re not carrying their burdens alone—that their sadness is woven into something much bigger.
This sense of collective melancholy runs deep in Istanbul’s history. Once the heart of a mighty empire, full of riches and power, the city now wears its past on its sleeve. You see hints of its former glory in old ruins scattered across the landscape, but you can’t help feeling the weight of what’s been lost. For folks who call this place home, that history is bittersweet—something to take pride in, but also a reason for sorrow. Sometimes, it’s hard not to wonder if the city’s brightest days are already behind it.
But here’s something important: hüzün isn’t just about missing the past. It’s also about facing the uncertainties of today, and somehow finding strength in them. In a city where change is always around the corner, and the future feels unpredictable, this shared sadness becomes a kind of resilience. People here learn to spot beauty even in decay, and they treasure those small, joyful moments that manage to shine through. You’ll find them gathering in cozy tea houses and bustling cafes, sharing stories, laughter, and a sense of togetherness that makes even the gloomiest day feel a little brighter.
For some, this melancholy actually sparks creativity. Artists and writers look at Istanbul’s contradictions and use hüzün as their lens. They see the ruins not just as leftovers from better times, but as proof of endurance—a sign that, despite everything, people keep adapting and moving forward. In their hands, the city’s sadness turns into art, transforming loss into something beautiful, something that celebrates what still remains.
If you’re not from here, it might be hard to understand what hüzün really means. You might just notice the city’s struggles on the surface, missing that deeper sense of connection that ties residents together. But for those who’ve grown up in Istanbul, this melancholy feels as familiar as the changing seasons. It shapes how people relate to each other, how they remember the past, and even how they imagine what’s ahead.
